Final report: Does Gerald Stern match all puzzle clues? Conclusion at a glance - Gerald Stern matches items (1), (2), (4a color), (4b city), and (6). - Evidence contradicts item (3) (father in produce). - Items (4c tightly sealed animal), (4d witness/spectator/onlooker/observer), (4e newspaper item), (5) documented 1990s meeting with Allen Ginsberg (needs a single source listing both at the same 1990s event), (7) drink-named magazine interview after 2022, and (8) pivot-synonym title remain unverified/not found. - Therefore, Stern does not match ALL clues. - Alternate candidate strongly suggested: Philip Lamantia (with sources). Detailed verification with sources, links, and quotes 1) Birth between 1900–1929 and lived into the 21st century — MATCHES - Poetry Foundation (Gerald Stern page): “Gerald Stern … 1925—2022 … Stern was born in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, in 1925.” Source: https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/gerald-stern - Academy of American Poets (Poets.org): “Gerald Stern … 1925 – 2022 … Stern lived in New Jersey and New York and died at the age of ninety-seven on October 28, 2022.” Source: https://poets.org/poet/gerald-stern 2) Child of immigrants (parents immigrated; confirm both) — MATCHES - Poetry Foundation: “The son of Eastern European immigrants.” Source: https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/gerald-stern - University of Pittsburgh, Archives & Special Collections, Finding Aid (biography section): “His parents, Harry and Ida Barach Stern, were Jewish immigrants from the Ukraine and Poland, respectively, who lived on Wylie Avenue in the city's Hill District…” Source: https://digital.library.pitt.edu/islandora/object/pitt:US-PPiU-sc200704/viewer - Wikipedia (with obituary ref): “His parents, Harry and Ida Barach Stern, were Jewish and immigrated to the United States from Ukraine and Poland, respectively, in 1905.” Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Stern 3) Father worked in produce (e.g., grocery/produce market) — DOES NOT MATCH - Wikipedia: “They owned several clothing stores and sold other items including cigars.” Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Stern - Note: I found no reputable source indicating his father worked in produce/grocery; available sources indicate retail clothing/cigars. 4) Poem titles that match specific categories - (a) A color — MATCHES - The Red Coal (poem title within his collection The Red Coal, 1981) - University of Pittsburgh Finding Aid (Subseries 5. The Red Coal): The subseries item list includes “The Red Coal.” The subseries description: “The Red Coal, published in 1981, earned Stern the Melville Caine Award.” Source: https://digital.library.pitt.edu/islandora/object/pitt:US-PPiU-sc200704/viewer - (b) A city — MATCHES - “It Was in Houston” (Poetry Foundation lists this poem): “From the magazine: It Was in Houston.” Source: https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/poems/36844/it-was-in-houston (also linked from Stern’s PF page) - Also: “Moscow” appears in Paradise Poems subseries content in the Pitt Finding Aid: list includes “Moscow.” Source: https://digital.library.pitt.edu/islandora/object/pitt:US-PPiU-sc200704/viewer - (c) A tightly sealed animal (e.g., “Canned Tuna”) — NOT FOUND - No Stern poem found with a title that is a sealed/canned animal in Poetry Foundation’s list or the Pitt finding aid’s poem lists. Sources: PF page https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/gerald-stern; Pitt finding aid https://digital.library.pitt.edu/islandora/object/pitt:US-PPiU-sc200704/viewer - (d) Someone who sees an event (e.g., “Witness,” “Spectator,” “Onlooker,” “Observer”) — NOT FOUND - No Stern poem titled with these terms in Poetry Foundation’s list or the Pitt finding aid. Sources as above. - (e) Something commonly found in newspapers (e.g., “Obituary,” “Headline,” “Classifieds”) — NOT FOUND - No such poem title found in the PF page or the Pitt finding aid lists. Sources as above. 5) A documented meeting with Allen Ginsberg in the 1990s — NOT CONFIRMED (partial context only) - Wikipedia (Geraldine R. Dodge Poetry Festival): “Among the poets who have participated in past festivals are … Allen Ginsberg … Gerald Stern … The Language of Life series was filmed at the 1994 Festival.” Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geraldine_R._Dodge_Poetry_Festival - Bill Moyers PBS page (The Language of Life): “filmed on location at the fifth biennial Geraldine R. Dodge Poetry Festival in historic Waterloo, New Jersey … Featured poets include …” (lists some featured poets for the series). Source: https://billmoyers.com/series/the-language-of-life-with-bill-moyers-1995/ - Assessment: These show both poets are documented Dodge participants, and the 1994 festival was filmed, but I did not locate a single authoritative source listing a specific 1990s event program where both Ginsberg and Stern appear together. This item remains unverified. 6) Statement that Stern was inspired by a particular artistic movement — MATCHES (Surrealism) - Poets.org (Academy of American Poets): “School/Movements — Surrealism” (on Stern’s page). Source: https://poets.org/poet/gerald-stern 7) After his death (2022), an article that includes an interview with him in a magazine named after a drink — NOT FOUND - A 2012 Q&A (pre-2022) exists at NJ.com: “Gerald Stern: A Q&A with New Jersey’s former poet laureate.” Source: https://www.nj.com/entertainment/arts/2012/11/gerald_stern_a_qa_with_new_jer.html - I did not find a post-2022 interview article in a drink-named magazine (Punch, Milk, Tea, Whiskey Island, etc.). 8) Poem title includes a synonym for a lever’s pivot (e.g., “fulcrum,” “pivot,” “axis,” “hinge”) — NOT FOUND - No such Stern poem title found via Poetry Foundation listings or the University of Pittsburgh finding aid poem lists. Sources: https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/gerald-stern; https://digital.library.pitt.edu/islandora/object/pitt:US-PPiU-sc200704/viewer Explicit matches vs. non-matches for Gerald Stern - Matches: (1), (2), (4a color), (4b city), (6) - Does not match: (3) - Not found/unverified after searching: (4c), (4d), (4e), (5), (7), (8) Next-best alternate candidate(s) with sources Philip Lamantia (strong match on multiple clues) - Birth window and lived into 21st century: “1927—2005.” Source: Poetry Foundation — https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/philip-lamantia - Child of immigrants: “Surrealist poet Philip Lamantia was born in San Francisco in 1927, the son of Sicilian immigrants.” Source: Poetry Foundation page above. - Movement inspiration: Core Surrealist figure (PF bio). - Poem titles: - Color: “Blue Grace” — listed by Poetry Foundation: https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/56435/blue-grace - City: “A Little Washington DC Dream” — Poetry Foundation: https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/56436/a-little-washington-dc-dream - Witness-type: “Witness” — Poetry Foundation: https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/56434/witness-56d238ecafca6 - Association with Allen Ginsberg: “Lamantia’s surrealist poetry influenced Allen Ginsberg and other Beat poets.” Source: Poetry Foundation — https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/philip-lamantia - Notes: Additional items (e.g., father in produce; drink-named magazine interview after 2022) are outside Lamantia’s scope (d. 2005), but he aligns with several title/period/movement clues. Confirmed 1925–2022; “son of Eastern European immigrants”; PF poem list including “It Was in Houston.” Source: https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/gerald-stern - Scraped Wikipedia – Gerald Stern: success. Confirmed parents immigrated (Ukraine/Poland, 1905) and family business: clothing stores and cigars (contradicts produce). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Stern - Attempted to scrape NYT obituary (403 Forbidden) and Pittsburgh Jewish Chronicle (403), and AP obituary (page loaded navigation; no usable quote retrieved). - Scraped Poets.org – Gerald Stern: success. Confirmed dates and “School/Movements: Surrealism.” Source: https://poets.org/poet/gerald-stern - Scraped NJ.com Q&A (2012): success. Verified a pre-2022 interview article; not applicable to the drink-magazine-after-2022 criterion. Source: https://www.nj.com/entertainment/arts/2012/11/gerald_stern_a_qa_with_new_jer.html - Scraped Poetry Foundation – Philip Lamantia: success. Confirmed “son of Sicilian immigrants,” Surrealism, poem titles “Blue Grace,” “A Little Washington DC Dream,” and “Witness”; note of influence on Allen Ginsberg. Source: https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/philip-lamantia - Scraped University of Pittsburgh finding aid – Gerald Stern Papers: success. Confirmed both parents were immigrants (Ukraine, Poland); verified poem and collection titles including The Red Coal and “Moscow.” Source: https://digital.library.pitt.edu/islandora/object/pitt:US-PPiU-sc200704/viewer - Attempted Dodge Poetry Festival site (SSL error); Wayback had no archive of target page. - Scraped Wikipedia – Dodge Poetry Festival: success. Confirmed both Allen Ginsberg and Gerald Stern among past participants; PBS filming of 1994 festival. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geraldine_R._Dodge_Poetry_Festival - Scraped Bill Moyers “The Language of Life” series page: success. Confirmed filming at the 5th Dodge Festival; lists some featured poets but not a complete roster including both Ginsberg and Stern. Source: https://billmoyers.com/series/the-language-of-life-with-bill-moyers-1995/ - Checked Wikipedia page for “Fooling with Words” (404), and an unrelated “The Language of Life” (music album) page (not applicable). Final answer Gerald Stern does not match all puzzle clues. - Matches: - (1) Born 1925 and lived into 21st century (d. 2022). Sources: Poetry Foundation; Poets.org. - (2) Child of immigrants; both parents immigrated (Ukraine and Poland). Sources: Poetry Foundation; University of Pittsburgh finding aid; Wikipedia. - (4a) Poem title that is a color: “The Red Coal” (poem within The Red Coal, 1981). Source: University of Pittsburgh finding aid. - (4b) Poem title that is a city: “It Was in Houston” (PF); also “Moscow” (Pitt finding aid). Sources: Poetry Foundation poem page; Pitt finding aid. - (6) Movement inspiration: Surrealism (explicitly listed under School/Movements). Source: Poets.org. - Does not match: - (3) Father worked in produce: Evidence indicates clothing/cigar retail, not produce. Source: Wikipedia. - Not found/unverified: - (4c) Tightly sealed animal title (e.g., “Canned Tuna”): Not found in reliable lists. - (4d) Someone who sees an event (e.g., “Witness,” “Spectator,” “Onlooker,” “Observer”): Not found for Stern (though available for alternate candidate Philip Lamantia). - (4e) Newspaper item title (e.g., “Obituary,” “Headline,” “Classifieds”): Not found for Stern. - (5) Documented meeting with Allen Ginsberg in the 1990s: Both documented Dodge participants; PBS filmed the 1994 festival, but I did not find a single source explicitly listing both together at the same 1990s event. Needs a specific official roster/program citation. - (7) Post-2022 interview article in a drink-named magazine: Not found. - (8) Poem title with “fulcrum/pivot/axis/hinge”: Not found. Suggested alternate candidate - Philip Lamantia satisfies multiple clues (1927–2005; son of Sicilian immigrants; Surrealism; poem titles that are a color “Blue Grace,” a city “A Little Washington DC Dream,” and a witness word “Witness”; associated with Allen Ginsberg). Sources: - Biography: “Surrealist poet Philip Lamantia … the son of Sicilian immigrants.” https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/philip-lamantia - Poems: Blue Grace; A Little Washington DC Dream; Witness (all at Poetry Foundation). - https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/56435/blue-grace - https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/56436/a-little-washington-dc-dream - https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/56434/witness-56d238ecafca6 - Ginsberg association: “Lamantia’s surrealist poetry influenced Allen Ginsberg and other Beat poets.” https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/philip-lamantia Notes on remaining gaps for Stern - For (5), seek an official Dodge Poetry Festival program (e.g., 1994 or 1996) or other institutional roster (archived or PDF) listing both Allen Ginsberg and Gerald Stern for the same year/date. - For (7), search archives of drink-named literary magazines (e.g., Whiskey Island, Milk, Tea, Punch) for memorial features post-October 2022, explicitly including interview content with Stern. - For (4c), (4d), (4e), and (8), consult complete tables of contents of collected/selected works and publisher catalog listings to confirm absence or discover any overlooked titles.

Part 1 — Poem identification and publication details - Title: Canned Tuna - Author: Tim Hunt - Source: Glass: A Journal of Poetry, Volume One, Issue Three - Date: December 2008 - Primary source (poem page): https://www.glass-poetry.com/volume-one/issue-three/hunt-tuna.html - Issue cover page with date: https://www.glass-poetry.com/volume-one/issue-three/cover.html - Quote (cover): “December 2008” - First lines (from poem page): - “In the photo he is seven or eight. Twine cinches his pants to his waist. His hair slicked back, he is smiling as if he wants the camera to like him but isn't sure it will. … Such differences are obvious, but they were then as much the ordinary as the canned tuna on toast the end of the month when I was a boy — not signs of making do. What was. That's the trick — to read what was.” Additional contemporaneous source info for the author from the same issue - Contributors page (Glass: A Journal of Poetry): https://www.glass-poetry.com/volume-one/issue-three/contributors.html - Quote (Tim Hunt): “My work has appeared in Coal Hill Review, Epoch, Quarterly West, Spoon River Poetry Review, Tar River Poetry and other journals. I’ve also published one chapbook (Lake County Diamond, Intertext Books). A full-length collection, The Land Must Eat, is to be published fall 2009 by The Backwaters Press.” Part 2 — Evaluation of the poet (Tim Hunt) against the seven puzzle clues Note: The puzzle asks whether the poet who authored the “tightly sealed animal” poem matches these clues. Page Title: Philip Lamantia Content: Philip Lamantia (October 23, 1927 – March 7, 2005) was an American poet, writer and lecturer. His poetry incorporated stylistic experimentation and transgressive themes, and has been regarded as surrealist and visionary, contributing to the literature of the Beat Generation. == Biography == Lamantia was born in San Francisco, California, United States, to Sicilian immigrants and was raised in the city's Excelsior District neighborhood. His poetry was first published in View magazine in 1943, when he was 15 years old, and his poetry appeared in the final issue of the Surrealist magazine VVV the following year. He dropped out of Balboa High School to pursue poetry in New York City, and appeared the same year in American filmmaker Maya Deren's At Land. Aged just 16, Lamantia was hailed by Andre Breton as "a voice that rises once in a hundred years". He returned to the Bay Area in 1945, and his first book, Erotic Poems, was published a year later. Lamantia was one of the post-World War II poets now sometimes referred to as the San Francisco Renaissance, and later became involved with the San Francisco Beat Generation poets and the Surrealist Movement in the United States. On October 7, 1955, he was on the bill at San Francisco's Six Gallery, where poet Allen Ginsberg read his poem Howl for the first time; at this event, Lamantia chose to read the poems of John Hoffman, a friend who had recently died. Gerd Stern, a poet who had met Lamantia at a reading at the San Francisco Museum of Art in 1947, recalled of his friend: "He admired Dylan Thomas and Wallace Stevens. He had a strange relationship with the surrealists. I could never get him to talk about it. In a way, it was not helping him with his reputation. He was very ambitious. In his last years, he returned to Catholicism and turned reclusive." Lamantia was also known for his journeys with native peoples in the United States and Mexico, participating in the peyote-eating rituals of the Washo Indians of Nevada, which often inspired his poems. In the 1950s, Lamantia wrote multiple political texts, including a polemical prose text criticizing federal prohibitions of drugs. After he re-embraced Catholicism in the later half of his life, his poetry onward began to explore Catholic themes. American writer Nancy Peters, who was Lamantia's wife and literary editor, commented that "he found in the narcotic night world a kind of modern counterpart to the Gothic castle—a zone of peril to be symbolically or existentially crossed." == Works == Erotic Poems (Berkeley: Bern Porter, 1946) Ekstasis (San Francisco: Auerhahn Press, 1959) Narcotica (San Francisco: Auerhahn Press, 1959) Destroyed Works (San Francisco: Auerhahn Press, 1962) Touch of the Marvelous ([no place] Oyez, 1966) Selected Poems 1943–1966 (San Francisco: City Lights Books, 1967) Charles Bukowski, Harold Norse, Philip Lamantia: Penguin Modern Poets, No. 13. (Harmondsworth: Penguin, 1969) Blood of the Air (San Francisco: Four Seasons Foundation, 1970) Touch of the Marvelous -- A New Edition (Bolinas: Four Seasons Foundation, 1974) Becoming Visible (San Francisco: City Lights Books, 1981) Meadowlark West (San Francisco: City Lights Books, 1986) Bed of Sphinxes: New and Selected Poems, 1943–1993 (San Francisco: City Lights Books, 1997) Tau; with Journey to the End by John Hoffman. Edited by Garrett Caples (San Francisco: City Lights Books, 2008) The Collected Poems of Philip Lamantia. Edited with an introduction by Garrett Caples, Andrew Joron, and Nancy Joyce Peters (Berkeley: University of California Press, 2013) Preserving Fire. Selected Prose. Edited with an introduction by Garrett Caples (Seattle/New York: Wave Books, 2018) Destroyed Works / Zerstörte Werke (German translation and afterword by Marcus Roloff, bilingual Edition. Wenzendorf: Stadtlichter Presse, 2021) == Notes == == References == Nancy Joyce Peters: Philip Lamantia. In: Dictionary of Literary Biography, Vol. 16, 330–336. Interview * [By Andrew Lundwall](https://litkicks.com/author/Andrew%20Lundwall/) * [April 8, 2006](https://litkicks.com/2006/04/08/) * [No Comments](https://litkicks.com/CaplesLamantia/#respond) * [Beat Generation](https://litkicks.com/category/beat-generation/), [Internet Culture](https://litkicks.com/category/internet-culture/), [Poetry](https://litkicks.com/category/Poetry/) *“Note: In July 2001, I was asked to interview Philip Lamantia for a local Bay Area magazine. It was meant to be a puff piece for a general audience, but Philip took it quite seriously as an opportunity to discuss his spiritual life and its relation to surrealism and poetry. He felt his views on Catholicism in particular had been misrepresented by a few unscrupulous journalists and wanted to set the record straight. But interviewing Philip was difficult. He spoke not in paragraphs but in volumes, with labrythine digressions which sometimes never returned to the ostensible subject at hand. We quickly had to abandon the ordinary Q&A approach in favor of his writing and phoning in various remarks, from which I reversed-engineered questions. While I assembled these discrete units into a plausibly conventional journalistic profile, he continued to refine his statements and, occasionally, change his mind, for he constantly interrogated his own beliefs. Paragraphs appeared and disappeared. As both deadline and word-count loomed, I managed to pull together a version that had his approval if not his entire confidence that I’d made him understood. The point, in any case, was moot, for the publisher deemed the discussion too esoteric for his target audience and promptly killed the piece. Not long afterward, in October, Lamantia fell into a lengthy depression from which he never fully recovered before his death on March 7, 2005 at age 77. To my knowledge, this is the last interview in which he participated.”* — [Garrett Caples](/GarrettCaples) Read Complete Interview [Here](http://www.angelfire.com/poetry/thepixelplus/nhlamantia.html). ## Leave a Reply Your email address will not be published.
